title: Fifty up, fifty down
hook: A price rises 50%, then falls 50%. Surely you are back where you started?

knows: what a percentage of a number is
the area of a rectangle is width times height
doesNotKnow: that successive percent changes multiply rather than add

misconception: A 50% rise followed by a 50% fall gets you back to where you started, because the two changes cancel.
objective: The learner can explain that a rise and a fall by the same percentage leave you below the start, because the fall is taken from the larger, risen amount: the result is (1 + p)(1 - p) = 1 - p^2 of the start.

claims.text: 100 raised by 50% is 150; 150 lowered by 50% is 75.
Up p% then down p% leaves (1 + p)(1 - p) = 1 - p^2 of the start, which is below the start for any p above zero.
Stage values: up 25% gives 125 then 93.75; up 50% gives 150 then 75; up 75% gives 175 then 43.75. The fall takes 31.25, 75 and 131.25; the net loss (the missing corner) is 6.25, 25 and 56.25.
claims.source: 100 x (1 + p) and 100 x (1 - p^2) for p = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75; corner 100 p^2. Recomputed with node.

claims.text: 10% up then 10% down ends at 99, a 1% net loss.

recall.question: A shop cuts a price by 20%, then raises the new price by 20%. Compared with the original price, it is now...
recall.why: The changes multiply: 0.8 x 1.2 = 0.96. The rise is 20% of a smaller base, so it does not undo the cut.
